This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 09 - Algorithmic Curation and Governance](../../Notebooks/Part%2009%20-%20Algorithmic%20Curation%20and%20Governance/Part%2009%20-%20Algorithmic%20Curation%20and%20Governance.ipynb).
On most platforms "the algorithm" is a sealed box that researchers audit
from outside, if at all. Bluesky decomposes curation into inspectable
parts — **feed generators**, **lists**, **starter packs**, and
**labelers** — all addressable through public endpoints. This part runs
a small *algorithm audit*: sampling posts from several custom feeds and
comparing what each one chooses to show.

### Learning objectives

* Enumerate feed generators and understand them as public records.
* Sample posts from custom feeds and build a comparable archive.
* Quantify feed composition: recency, engagement, concentration, media.
* Inspect lists, starter packs, and moderation labels.
* Frame audits of curation systems without platform cooperation.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)

BSKY_APP_DID <- "did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur"  # bsky.app
BSKY_MOD_DID <- "did:plc:ar7c4by46qjdydhdevvrndac"  # moderation.bsky.app
```

## 1. Feed generators are public records

A custom feed is itself a record in its creator's repository — with a
name, a description, and a like count of subscribers. Everything
`bsky.app` publishes, via [`bs_get_feeds()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feeds.html) (each bskyr function
links to its reference page on first use):

```{r actor-feeds}
bsky_feeds <- bs_get_feeds("bsky.app", limit = 50)

bsky_feeds |>
  select(display_name, like_count, description) |>
  arrange(desc(like_count))
```

[`bs_get_feed_generators()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feed_generators.html) resolves any batch of feed URIs to their metadata, so
audits can name exactly which version of which algorithm they sampled:

```{r generators}
CANDIDATE_FEEDS <- c(
  "Discover" = paste0("at://", BSKY_APP_DID,
                      "/app.bsky.feed.generator/whats-hot"),
  "What's Hot Classic" = paste0("at://", BSKY_APP_DID,
                                "/app.bsky.feed.generator/hot-classic"),
  "Science" = "at://did:plc:jfhpnnst6flqway4eaeqzj2a/app.bsky.feed.generator/for-science",
  "News" = "at://did:plc:kkf4naxqmweop7dv4l2iqqf5/app.bsky.feed.generator/verified-news"
)

generators <- bs_get_feed_generators(unname(CANDIDATE_FEEDS))

generators |>
  select(display_name, creator_handle, like_count)
```

## 2. Sampling posts from custom feeds

[`bs_get_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_feed.html) returns what a feed generator is serving right now. Like
Part 07, we take the raw response (`clean = FALSE`) so that whatever
embed types the feeds surface cannot break us, and flatten just the
fields the audit needs. Note the bookkeeping that makes an audit an
audit: every sample records *when it was retrieved*, because a feed is a
moving target and "the Discover feed" without a timestamp is not a
defined object:

```{r fetch-feeds}
feed_posts <- function(uri, target = 150) {
  pages <- tryCatch(bs_get_feed(uri, limit = target, clean = FALSE),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(pages)) return(NULL)
  items <- list_flatten(map(pages, "feed"))
  map(items, \(item) {
    post <- item$post
    embed_type <- post$embed$`$type` %||% ""
    tibble(
      uri = post$uri,
      author_did = post$author$did,
      author_handle = post$author$handle,
      created_at = post$record$createdAt %||% NA_character_,
      like_count = post$likeCount %||% 0L,
      repost_count = post$repostCount %||% 0L,
      has_media = str_detect(embed_type, "images|video")
    )
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

samples <- imap(CANDIDATE_FEEDS, \(uri, name) {
  retrieved_at <- now("UTC")
  posts <- feed_posts(uri)
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  if (is.null(posts)) return(NULL)
  mutate(posts, feed = name, retrieved_at = retrieved_at)
})

map_int(compact(samples), nrow)
```

### A no-algorithm baseline

Audits need a reference point. A *list feed* — the reverse-chronological
posts of a fixed roster — has no ranking algorithm at all. We find
`bsky.app`'s curation list with [`bs_get_actor_lists()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_actor_lists.html) and read its
feed with [`bs_get_list_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_list_feed.html):

```{r baseline}
bsky_lists <- bs_get_actor_lists("bsky.app", limit = 50) |>
  bsky_standardize()   # same column names under bskyr 0.4.x and 0.5.0

baseline_list <- bsky_lists |>
  filter(str_detect(purpose, "curatelist")) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)

baseline_posts <- NULL
if (nrow(baseline_list) == 1) {
  pages <- bs_get_list_feed(baseline_list$uri, limit = 150, clean = FALSE)
  items <- list_flatten(map(pages, "feed"))
  baseline_posts <- map(items, \(item) {
    post <- item$post
    embed_type <- post$embed$`$type` %||% ""
    tibble(uri = post$uri, author_did = post$author$did,
           author_handle = post$author$handle,
           created_at = post$record$createdAt %||% NA_character_,
           like_count = post$likeCount %||% 0L,
           repost_count = post$repostCount %||% 0L,
           has_media = str_detect(embed_type, "images|video"))
  }) |> list_rbind() |>
    mutate(feed = "Baseline (list feed)", retrieved_at = now("UTC"))
}

# list_rbind() stacks a list of tibbles; compact() drops feeds that failed
posts_df <- list_rbind(compact(c(samples, list(baseline_posts)))) |>
  mutate(created_at = ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE),
         age_hours = as.numeric(difftime(retrieved_at, created_at,
                                         units = "hours")))

count(posts_df, feed)
```

```{r save-archive}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(posts_df, "data/feed_posts.rds")
write_csv(posts_df, "data/feed_posts.csv")
```

## 3. Auditing feed composition

For each feed: how fresh are its posts, how engaged, how concentrated on
few authors, how visual? Concentration gets two measures. The
*top-10-author share* is intuitive: what fraction of the feed comes from
its ten most frequent authors? The **Herfindahl–Hirschman index** (HHI),
borrowed from antitrust economics, is the sum of squared author shares:
it approaches 1 when one author dominates and 1/n when posts are spread
evenly over n authors:

```{r composition}
hhi <- function(authors) {
  shares <- table(authors) / length(authors)
  sum(shares^2)
}

comparison <- posts_df |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(
    posts = n(),
    unique_authors = n_distinct(author_did),
    top10_author_share = {
      top <- head(sort(table(author_did), decreasing = TRUE), 10)
      sum(top) / n()
    },
    hhi = hhi(author_did),
    median_age_hours = median(age_hours, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_likes = median(like_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    media_share = mean(has_media)
  )

write_csv(comparison, "data/feed_comparison.csv")
comparison
```

```{r composition-plots, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
posts_df |>
  filter(age_hours > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(age_hours, color = feed)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Post age at retrieval (hours)",
       y = "Cumulative share of posts",
       title = "Recency profile of each feed") +
  theme_minimal()

posts_df |>
  ggplot(aes(like_count + 1, color = feed)) +
  stat_ecdf() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Likes at retrieval (+1)", y = "Cumulative share of posts",
       title = "Engagement profile of each feed") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### What the differences reveal

Before interpreting, one small table puts each feed's median likes next
to the baseline's (with +1 smoothing, so a baseline median of 0 can't
divide by zero):

```{r contrasts}
baseline_likes <- comparison$median_likes[comparison$feed == "Baseline (list feed)"]

comparison |>
  transmute(feed, median_likes, median_age_hours, top10_author_share,
            unique_authors,
            likes_vs_baseline = if (length(baseline_likes) == 1)
              (median_likes + 1) / (baseline_likes + 1) else NA_real_)
```

The magnitudes are live and will differ from run to run; the logic
behind each contrast is what's stable:

* **Engagement depends on what a feed selects on.** Discover and What's
  Hot Classic rank posts by popularity signals, so their posts' like
  counts sit above the baseline's — usually far above, in Discover's
  case. The feed conditions on engagement; it didn't cause it. The
  allowlist feeds (Science, News) instead admit posts from a vetted
  roster, so their median likes can sit near, or even below, the
  baseline's: an "algorithmic" feed isn't necessarily an
  engagement-ranked one.
* **Recency is a design choice.** Some feeds serve posts only minutes
  old, others posts a few hours old;
  the list baseline simply mirrors its roster's posting rhythm, which for
  a quiet roster reaches days into the past.
* **Concentration reflects the eligible population.** The allowlist
  feeds draw on a vetted roster, so a few prolific accounts can supply a
  large share of their posts; the baseline, with only a handful of
  members, is concentrated by construction.

None of this required platform cooperation — only public endpoints and
a sampling design.

## 4. Audience overlap between feeds

Do different feeds show the same *accounts*? **Jaccard similarity** —
the size of the intersection of two author sets divided by the size of
their union — runs from 0 (no shared authors) to 1 (identical author
sets). tidyr's `crossing()` builds every pair of feeds, and
`pivot_wider()` arranges the result as a matrix. We write
`tidyr::crossing()` with the package name because igraph, which Parts 03
and 04 load, has a different function also called `crossing()`; if
igraph is still attached in your R session, the plain name would call
the wrong one:

```{r jaccard}
author_sets <- posts_df |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(authors = list(unique(author_did)))

jaccard <- function(a, b) length(intersect(a, b)) / length(union(a, b))

tidyr::crossing(f1 = author_sets$feed, f2 = author_sets$feed) |>
  mutate(jaccard = map2_dbl(
    f1, f2,
    \(x, y) jaccard(author_sets$authors[[match(x, author_sets$feed)]],
                    author_sets$authors[[match(y, author_sets$feed)]])
  )) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = f2, values_from = jaccard)
```

Near-zero overlaps mean the feeds are sampling almost disjoint slices of
the network — each algorithm is a different *editorial regime*. Which
pairs overlap at all, and by how much, changes from run to run, but even
the largest overlaps in a snapshot tend to be a small fraction of either
feed's authors.

## 5. Lists: shared rosters for curation and moderation

Lists are public records too — rosters that anyone can subscribe to as a
feed, or (for modlists) as a mute/block set. [`bs_get_list()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_list.html) reads a
list's members:

```{r lists}
bsky_lists |>
  transmute(name, purpose = str_extract(purpose, "[^#]+$"),
            members = as.integer(list_item_count),
            description = str_trunc(replace_na(description, ""), 80))

if (nrow(baseline_list) == 1) {
  members <- bs_get_list(baseline_list$uri, limit = 200)
  members |> select(subject_handle, subject_display_name) |> head(10)
}
```

## 6. Starter packs: curating the network itself

Starter packs bundle accounts (and feeds) so newcomers can follow an
entire community at once — curation of the *graph*, not of content.
[`bs_get_actor_starter_packs()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_actor_starter_packs.html) lists an account's packs with counts of
how many users joined through each, this week and all time. (This
summary view doesn't say how many accounts a pack contains; for that you
would fetch the pack itself, as Exercise 4 asks.) `bsky_standardize()`
from `bsky_client.R` gives the count columns the same names whichever
bskyr version you have installed:

```{r starter-packs}
packs <- bs_get_actor_starter_packs("bsky.app", limit = 50) |>
  bsky_standardize()

packs |>
  select(record_name, joined_week_count, joined_all_time_count) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("joined"), as.integer)) |>   # counts can arrive as text
  arrange(desc(joined_all_time_count))
```

### Starter packs as a natural experiment

Joining through a pack assigns a newcomer hundreds of follows in one
click — a discontinuity in initial conditions that Part 05's designs can
exploit: compare the retention and activity of accounts that joined
through different packs.

## 7. Labels and stackable moderation

Moderation on Bluesky is *stackable*: independent labeler services emit
labels (like `spam` or `graphic-media`) that clients can subscribe to
and act on. The labels themselves are queryable from each labeler.
bskyr has no wrapper for this endpoint, which is a teachable moment in
itself: any XRPC endpoint is just an HTTP URL, so we build the request
directly with [httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org) against Bluesky's own
moderation service at `https://mod.bsky.app` (see the
[`queryLabels` reference](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/comatprotolabel/GET/xrpc/com.atproto.label.queryLabels)).

Our `query_labels()` sends the patterns in batches of 25 per request,
pauses between requests, caps the number of requests, and collects the
labels from every batch into one tibble. One design
choice deserves attention before we use it: if the labeler **refuses** a
request, the function stops with an error that carries the labeler's own
explanation, instead of quietly returning an empty table. A refused
request and a request that found nothing both "return no labels", but
only one of them is a finding. `httr2::req_error(body = ...)` is what
pulls the server's message into the error:

```{r labels}
query_labels <- function(patterns, labeler = "https://mod.bsky.app",
                         batch_size = 25, max_requests = 20) {
  batches <- split(patterns, ceiling(seq_along(patterns) / batch_size))
  if (length(batches) > max_requests) {
    message("Querying only the first ", max_requests, " of ",
            length(batches), " batches")
    batches <- head(batches, max_requests)
  }
  labels <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(batches)) {
    resp <- httr2::request(paste0(labeler, "/xrpc/com.atproto.label.queryLabels")) |>
      httr2::req_url_query(uriPatterns = batches[[i]], limit = 250, .multi = "explode") |>
      httr2::req_error(body = \(r) c(
        tryCatch(httr2::resp_body_json(r)$message, error = \(e) NULL),
        sprintf("(%s refused label query batch %d of %d)", labeler, i, length(batches))
      )) |>
      httr2::req_perform() |>
      httr2::resp_body_json()
    labels <- c(labels, resp$labels)
    Sys.sleep(0.2)
  }
  tibble(uri = map_chr(labels, "uri"),
         val = map_chr(labels, "val"),
         neg = map_lgl(labels, \(l) isTRUE(l$neg)))
}

post_uris <- head(unique(posts_df$uri), 300)
post_labels <- query_labels(post_uris)
nrow(post_labels)
```

Labels are usually sparse on curated-feed posts, because curation and
moderation interact: most labeled content never *reaches* a feed, and
what the AppView has taken down we never see at all. A label does not
delete anything, either — when labeled posts do appear, they sit in the
feed with their label attached, and each user's client decides whether
to hide, blur, or show them.

To confirm the labeler is far from idle, we'd like to widen the query to
the *accounts* that wrote these posts. The `queryLabels` lexicon allows
wildcard patterns like `at://did:plc:.../*`, meaning "any record in this
account's history", and an earlier version of this document used
exactly that. Let's see what the moderation service says to one today.
`tryCatch()` catches the error so that we can print it rather than stop
the document:

```{r wildcard-demo}
example_did <- posts_df$author_did[1]

tryCatch({
  wildcard <- query_labels(paste0("at://", example_did, "/*"))
  cat("Wildcard queries work again:", nrow(wildcard), "labels in one account history.\n")
}, error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
```

In 2026 Bluesky's moderation service stopped accepting wildcard queries,
answering every one with *"Support for wildcard label queries is
temporarily disabled"*. (If the chunk above reports that they work
again, the service has re-enabled them; the rest of this section works
either way.) This is the "platform in flux" lesson in its purest form:
nothing in our code changed, and the API reference still describes
wildcards, but a measurement that worked one month stopped working the
next. The earlier version of this document didn't check, and reported
**"No labels found in this sample"** — a confident empirical claim
produced by a refused request. That is why `query_labels()` now stops
with the server's message instead.

So we ask the questions that *can* still be asked, with two kinds of
pattern the service accepts:

* **(a) Labels on the accounts themselves.** A bare DID as the pattern
  returns labels applied to the account, as opposed to any one of its
  posts.
* **(b) Labels on their recent posts.** For 20 of the sampled authors we
  fetch their latest 30 feed items with [`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html), keep the
  original posts (the `is_repost()` and `is_reply()` helpers from
  `bsky_client.R`), and query those exact URIs. This covers only a
  recent window rather than a whole history, so its counts are lower
  bounds on what a full history would show.

```{r history-labels}
set.seed(42)
sampled_dids <- sample(unique(posts_df$author_did),
                       min(50, n_distinct(posts_df$author_did)))

# (a) one bare DID per pattern
account_labels <- query_labels(sampled_dids) |> filter(!neg)  # drop retracted labels

# (b) exact URIs of recent original posts by 20 of those authors
recent_uris <- map(head(sampled_dids, 20), \(did) {
  feed <- tryCatch(bs_get_author_feed(did, limit = 30),
                   error = \(e) NULL)   # a deleted or suspended account has no feed
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  if (is.null(feed) || nrow(feed) == 0) return(character())
  feed$uri[!is_repost(feed) & !is_reply(feed)]
}) |> list_c()
recent_labels <- query_labels(recent_uris, max_requests = 40) |> filter(!neg)

cat("(a) Labels on the", length(sampled_dids), "sampled accounts:", nrow(account_labels), "\n")
account_labels |> count(val, sort = TRUE)
cat("(b) Labels on", length(recent_uris), "recent posts by 20 authors:", nrow(recent_labels), "\n")
recent_labels |> count(val, sort = TRUE)

# Put the post samples on a common scale: active labels per 100 posts
per_100 <- function(labels, n_posts) if (n_posts > 0) 100 * sum(!labels$neg) / n_posts else NA_real_
c(feed_posts = per_100(post_labels, length(post_uris)),
  authors_recent_posts = per_100(recent_labels, length(recent_uris))) |> round(1)
```

Compare the two rates in the last line, and notice how few labels sit
behind each. With a few hundred posts and labels this sparse, a handful
of labeled posts decides which rate is higher, and reruns come out both
ways — so the comparison is a design for a study, not yet a finding.
Two things *are* stable: account-level labels are a different kind of
judgment (flags about an account rather than any one post), and the
post labels that appear are mostly content-classification labels such
as `sexual`, `porn`, and `graphic-media`, which drive the warnings users
configure rather than removing anything. The pattern used here (exact URIs for
your sample; account DIDs and recent-post URIs for context) is a
reusable template for studying *label prevalence*. Remember, though,
that a label is a moderation *action*: a row saying an account was
labeled `rude` is an allegation attached to an identity, so report
prevalence in aggregate.

## 8. Reproducibility: working from the saved archive

```{r reload}
archive <- readRDS("data/feed_posts.rds")

archive |>
  group_by(feed) |>
  summarise(median_likes = median(like_count),
            median_reposts = median(repost_count))
```

## 9. Research design: algorithm audits without platform cooperation

The audit tradition (Sandvig et al. 2014) had to scrape or run sock
puppets because platforms hid their rankers; Bluesky's architecture
makes the *outputs* of every public feed generator directly observable.
What remains unobservable is *personalization*: feeds that rank
relative to a logged-in user can only be audited from that user's
standpoint — exactly the layer Huszár et al. (2022) needed internal
Twitter access to study. A serious audit samples feeds repeatedly over
time, archives everything with retrieval timestamps, and reports the
sampling design alongside the findings.

## Ethics and limitations

Feed samples are snapshots: the same feed an hour later serves different
posts, so archive retrieval times and treat comparisons as
time-specific. Posts surfaced by feeds were written by people who never
chose to be in your sample — the usual minimization rules apply. Label
data is moderation data: publishing which accounts carry which labels
can amplify harm, so aggregate. Survivorship matters too: the AppView
filters taken-down content before we ever see it, which is part of why
labels are sparse on feed posts. The platform is also in flux — feed
rosters, labeler policies, and even which queries a labeler accepts
change, as the wildcard episode showed. And remember the deepest limitation:
without logged-in vantage points, personalized curation is invisible.

## Exercises

1. Add a topical feed you use to `CANDIDATE_FEEDS` and rerun the audit.
   Where does it fall on concentration and recency?
2. Sample the Discover feed three times, an hour apart, and measure the
   Jaccard overlap of its post sets — how fast does the feed churn?
3. Compute author-level Gini coefficients per feed as an alternative
   concentration measure.
4. Unpack the most-joined starter pack's list members and check how many
   also appear in the feed samples.
5. Compare label prevalence across feeds: group `posts_df` by feed,
   query each feed's post URIs (and its authors' recent posts) separately,
   and report labels per 100 posts per feed.

## Research project ideas

* **A longitudinal feed observatory.** Sample a fixed set of feeds daily
  for a month, archiving composition metrics; characterize how editorial
  regimes drift and respond to news events.
* **Starter-pack cohorts.** Identify accounts that joined via packs
  (join counts are public), build matched cohorts (Part 05), and
  estimate the causal effect of initial follow endowments on retention.
